claims.text: Traditional fusion-welding repair is ineffective for damaged Inconel 718 because of hot-cracking risk.
Optimized friction stir processing can repair a damaged Inconel 718 component without melting it.
The proposed FSP peak-temperature range is typically 600–800°C.
FSP induces severe plastic deformation while remaining below the melting point.
The deformation imposed by FSP triggers dynamic recrystallization.
FSP will create a refined and homogeneous microstructure in the processed Inconel 718 region.
FSP-induced microstructural evolution will heal pre-existing defects and grain boundaries.
FSP eliminates slow-cooling zones that could foster hot cracking.
The refined microstructure improves grain-boundary integrity.
Improved grain-boundary integrity increases resistance to crack initiation under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses.
Improved grain-boundary integrity increases resistance to crack propagation under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses.
FSP repair will eliminate hot cracking in the repaired Inconel 718 region.
FSP-repaired specimens will exhibit later crack initiation than fusion-weld-repaired specimens.
FSP-repaired specimens will exhibit lower crack-propagation rates than fusion-weld-repaired specimens.
FSP-repaired specimens will have greater fatigue life and mechanical integrity than fusion-weld-repaired specimens.
The predicted repair advantage applies at approximately 700°C under high cyclic mechanical loads.
The predicted results require an optimized non-melting process window with minimized residual stresses.
Fusion-welded Inconel 718 repairs have inferior fatigue performance under the stated aggressive service conditions.
Optimized FSP parameters from analogous materials may not transfer uniformly to Inconel 718, particularly for residual-stress control and complex geometries.
